source.title: OTIS: Learning High-Quality Time Series Features With Tiny Encoders
source.authors: Ö. Turgut; Philip Müller; M. Menten; Daniel Rueckert

record.file_problem: Minor OCR and formatting artifacts; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps time-series encoder size and pretraining-data size, and reports that downstream performance improves with more data but nearly saturates with larger encoders. This refines the broader scaling claim in a different domain, although it does not measure language-model loss.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling laws as motivation, but does not test held-out language-model cross-entropy, small-run extrapolation, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its own scaling results are downstream-task measurements for time-series encoders. Rows record the aggregate trends explicitly described in Section 5.4; task-specific plotted values are not readable as numbers in the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The study scales its own masked-modelling time-series encoder in pretraining data (1%, 10%, 100%) and in parameters (7.1M, 40M, 116M) and reports downstream results. That is a result on downstream scaling (V6) in a new, non-language setting. It fits no loss curve and no power law, so V1-V5 and V7 are not tested. T3 fits better than T5: the scaling analysis is a side experiment on the authors' own method, not a targeted argument against a version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors find that downstream performance scales reliably with pretraining data but saturates with encoder size. They attribute the plateau to redundancy in time-series data and say scaling time-series encoders needs further engineering. Their main claim is that targeted inductive biases let a 7.1M encoder match much larger encoders such as MOMENT-386M.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains time-series encoders and measures downstream-task performance across data and model sizes; it does not use language-model held-out cross-entropy, loss-law fitting, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream performance is reported to vary with pretraining-data size and to show little benefit from larger encoder configurations.
record.problems: The scaling experiment reports downstream metrics for three selected tasks rather than held-out pretraining loss. The section's per-condition results are presented as plots without numeric values in the supplied text, limiting exact comparison.
record.rows_left_out: No results left out; task-specific numeric values from Figure 8 are not available in the supplied text, so only the aggregate trends stated by the authors are recorded.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss and no power-law fit in parameters, data or compute.
Shape is not varied at a fixed parameter count; the Large and Huge models change depth and width together with size.
Time-series is another modality, but neither pretraining loss nor a power-law form is measured.

Language-model downstream tasks are not tested. Prediction from pretraining loss is not tested. Predictability in the quantitative sense (a fitted trend) is not tested, since there are only three data points per axis.
No comparison of exponents or fitting methods.

record.verdict_notes: The headline comparison with MOMENT-386M and UniTS (Tables 1-4, 19) compares different models trained with different recipes, not a scaling test, so it was correctly left out of the rows. The rows also bear on V6 only under a broad reading of it, since V6's original context is language models. A stricter reading would move them to fits_no_version. The size sweep is small (one order of magnitude), all sizes ran 200 epochs, and the Large and Huge models used different learning rates and batch sizes. These limits weaken the parameter-plateau result.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law fits in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No extrapolation from small runs to larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation experiment or parameter/token optima.
No controlled comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The paper evaluates time-series encoders, but does not measure whether the same power-law form holds for their pretraining loss or in other training regimes.
Tests downstream performance against pretraining-data and encoder size in time-series encoders; does not test language-model downstream tasks or prediction from pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitting methods, exponents, parameter-count conventions, or compute-optimal splits. The reported size plateau is in downstream time-series metrics, not fitted loss curves.

relationships.reason: Downstream ACC, R2 and MSE improve consistently as the corpus grows, on Epilepsy, LVSV and ETTm2 (r1-r3). This is monotone over three points only, with no fit.

labels.condition: Parameter scaling from 7.1M to 40M and 116M in time-series encoders, with per-size hyperparameters not matched
labels.reason: The authors explicitly describe almost no downstream advantage for larger encoders (r4–r6). The rules classify negligible effects as absent and absence within the named condition group as challenges. Different hyperparameters constrain causal attribution.

relation.reason: The study directly varies pretraining-data quantity and encoder size and measures downstream performance.

tranche.reason: Section 5.4 explicitly reports negligible downstream advantage from increasing encoder size, qualifying V6. Under the stated definitions, this warrants T5 despite the new time-series setting.

source_check.notes: Figure 8 labels the three sample counts 6,123, 61,239 and 612,394, whereas Section 4 and Appendix A describe a total corpus of approximately 640k (640,187). The scaling results are qualitative three-point trends; plotted task values are not numerically tabulated.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Increasing pretraining-data size in the tested time-series encoder configurations
reader_labels.reason: The authors report consistent downstream gains as the corpus grows from 1% to 100% (r1-r3); they do not fit or establish a power law.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Increasing encoder size from 7.1 M to 40 M or 116 M parameters in the tested time-series tasks
reader_labels.reason: The larger configurations provide almost no downstream-performance advantage over the base encoder (r4-r6), so downstream gains do not reliably follow parameter scale in this setting.
